stories.headline: OpenAI launches GPT-6 Cyber and rates it "Critical" for cyber risk
stories.script: Our lead story today. OpenAI has launched GPT-6 Cyber, a model built to discover and confirm exploitable weaknesses in software while keeping within the boundaries a security researcher defines. Under its own safety framework, the company classifies the model's cyber capability as "Critical". As a result, access is currently limited to chosen customers in its Daybreak Red programme, via the API and Codex, though OpenAI intends to broaden availability over the next few weeks. According to the company, the model uncovered 81 high-severity vulnerabilities in Firefox that had not been known before. It also achieved 48.5 percent on OpenAI's ExploitGym benchmark, compared with 32.1 percent for GPT-5.6 Cyber. Those results come from OpenAI itself.
stories.whyThisMatters: OpenAI has launched GPT-6 Cyber, a model built to discover and confirm exploitable weaknesses in software while keeping within the boundaries a security researcher defines.
keyPoints: OpenAI launches GPT-6 Cyber and rates it "Critical" for cyber risk

stories.headline: METR finds AI is helping Anthropic improve its models about twice as fast
stories.script: Also today. The independent evaluator METR has released an assessment of Anthropic's internal research covering August to October. METR estimates that the capabilities of Anthropic's models are advancing roughly 1.9 times faster than they did between March 2024 and October 2025. It says AI tools that accelerate employees' coding and experimental work likely explain most of that gain. METR said it saw no obvious constraint that would prevent further acceleration within the next year. However, Anthropic blacked out much of the evidence METR regarded as most revealing, pointing to competitive confidentiality, which means the full grounds for the findings cannot be verified publicly. If AI is now hastening the creation of its own successors, progress could speed up sharply, raising the stakes for independent measurement and openness.
stories.whyThisMatters: The independent evaluator METR has released an assessment of Anthropic's internal research covering August to October.
keyPoints: METR finds AI is helping Anthropic improve its models about twice as fast

stories.headline: Google sued over suicide-related AI chats on school computer
stories.script: In other news. Google is being sued by the parents of a 13-year-old girl, according to The Economic Times. They allege that she used the company's AI technology, on a computer provided by her school, to plan a possible suicide and her own funeral. AI developers in the United States face a growing number of similar cases. OpenAI is contesting several wrongful death lawsuits, including one brought by the parents of Adam Raine, a 16-year-old who allegedly took his own life using methods suggested by ChatGPT.
stories.whyThisMatters: Google is being sued by the parents of a 13-year-old girl, according to The Economic Times.
keyPoints: Google sued over suicide-related AI chats on school computer

stories.headline: China cracks down on AI fakes that impersonate celebrities
stories.script: In China. The Cyberspace Administration of China, the country's internet regulator, says it has taken down more than 47,000 posts and punished 3,961 accounts that used artificial intelligence to pose as celebrities, China Daily reports. The crackdown focuses on AI-generated faces and voices used to deceive the public or promote products. With convincing deepfakes now cheap to produce, impersonation of famous people has become a large-scale problem, and regulators are beginning to target the accounts behind it as well as the content itself.

stories.headline: India's CERT-In asks organisations to audit what their AI agents can access and do
stories.script: Turning to India. CERT-In, India's national cybersecurity agency, has urged organisations to check whether their AI agents could leak confidential data or take actions they were never permitted to perform, The Times of India reports. The agency's AI security auditing guidelines call for strict controls on permissions, a log of every step an agent takes, an emergency mechanism to halt an agent, and sign-off from a human before any significant action. The guidance also addresses prompt injection, in which harmful instructions concealed in documents, emails or web pages attempt to hijack an agent. Indian companies are beginning to let AI agents reach email, files, internal systems and financial data, and the guidelines treat agent permissions and audit records as a core security safeguard from the outset.

stories.headline: NATO opens a counter-drone marketplace as Shield AI agrees to buy Echodyne
stories.script: Around the world. NATO's communications agency has launched a marketplace where allied nations can buy from a list of 16 pre-approved counter-drone systems, without having to hold tenders of their own, AeroTime reports. An additional 3.1 million euros has been earmarked for more testing. The French company Alta Ares, which develops interceptors powered by artificial intelligence, says it secured six of the 16 lots. In a separate deal, Shield AI, the company behind the Hivemind AI pilot, has agreed to acquire radar manufacturer Echodyne to bolster its counter-drone offerings. Drones have pushed rapid, AI-assisted air defence up military agendas, and NATO is now buying that capability off a prepared catalogue, much as governments purchase software.

stories.headline: Russia and US seek to block plan for binding rules on autonomous weapons
stories.script: In other news. A group of countries led by Russia and the United States is working to derail talks on legally binding rules for autonomous weapons, the Guardian reports. The two nations plan to use a United Nations conference later this month to block the proposals. Many observers see the meeting as a turning point after years of dispute over how weapons run by artificial intelligence should be governed, and efforts to close that gap in regulation now appear at risk. The extent of the opposition is likely to become clear at a diplomatic retreat beginning on Friday. That meeting precedes the seventh review conference on certain conventional weapons, which is scheduled to be held in Geneva from 16 to 20 November. 128 countries are expected to attend.
stories.whyThisMatters: A group of countries led by Russia and the United States is working to derail talks on legally binding rules for autonomous weapons, the Guardian reports.
keyPoints: Russia and US seek to block plan for binding rules on autonomous weapons

stories.headline: Nigel Farage's exit from the Telegraph may be cause for cheer. But there’s a sobering side to this story | Jane Martinson
stories.script: Next. Writing in the Guardian, commentator Jane Martinson argues that Nigel Farage's departure from the Daily Telegraph has a more troubling side. In her view, the turmoil at the paper seems driven less by politics than by a move toward artificial intelligence, with journalism ultimately bearing the cost. Farage had written a column for the Telegraph since 2016. Much of that writing promoted the party he leads, first the Brexit party and now Reform UK, or accused his opponents of weakness on immigration. The cash-strapped paper paid him roughly £4,000 a month, close to half a million pounds over the past ten years. This week it emerged that Axel Springer, the Telegraph's new German owner, had opted not to continue his columns. People close to Farage, though, maintain that the decision to go was his own.

stories.headline: VFlash: Fast, Accurate Visual Planning via Flash Primitive Decoding
stories.script: From the research desk. In a paper titled VFlash: Fast, Accurate Visual Planning via Flash Primitive Decoding, the researchers take on a speed problem in the AI that guides robots and self-driving cars. These systems can plan visually as well as in words, marking targets and predicting movement using points, boxes drawn around objects, and paths. Current vision-language models, which pair image understanding with text, produce such plans one coordinate at a time, so more detailed plans take longer. VFlash takes advantage of the predictable shapes of these visual elements to work out all of their coordinates at once, relying on a small assistant model that sketches an entire element in a single step.
stories.whyThisMatters: In a paper titled VFlash: Fast, Accurate Visual Planning via Flash Primitive Decoding, the researchers take on a speed problem in the AI that guides robots and self-driving cars.
keyPoints: VFlash: Fast, Accurate Visual Planning via Flash Primitive Decoding
